prize_parts.citation: For developing targeted protein degradation, from heterobifunctional PROTACs to the cereblon-mediated mechanism of molecular glue degraders

statement.case_for: Targeted protein degradation turns small molecules into programmable effectors of ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis. The two halves of the story fit together: Crews and Deshaies conceived and demonstrated heterobifunctional PROTACs, and Handa identified cereblon as the thalidomide target, which explained molecular glues and gave the field a mechanistic basis. The chemistry is the point, in linker and ligand design, ternary-complex formation and induced proximity. It also reframes what a drug can be, since it removes a protein rather than inhibiting it. The mechanism has been reproduced in many laboratories, and degraders are in clinical trials with early human proof-of-concept. Four of the eight opening ballots put it in the top four, and it is the only candidate every member ranked, which suggests a broad base of support. That breadth does not by itself prove merit, so I rest the case on originality and mechanistic depth.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is timing. No degrader has yet been approved, so the clinical payoff is still prospective. Attribution is also crowded: Ciulli (VHL ligands, structural design), Gray, Sakamoto and Ito all made important contributions, and a three-person cut will leave out people whose work was decisive for the field's chemistry. The prize could also be read as conflating two achievements, PROTAC design and the thalidomide-cereblon mechanism, which are conceptually related but historically distinct.

responses.point: Linke ranks sequencing-by-synthesis first and the Crews/Deshaies/Ciulli version of the degradation prize fourth, treating the thalidomide-glue story (Handa, Ito) as a separate matter.
responses.response: I agree sequencing chemistry is a real chemical achievement, and Balasubramanian and Klenerman are a clean pair. I still think the glue story cannot be left out of a degradation prize. Without Handa's identification of cereblon, the molecular-glue half of the field has no mechanism, and the clinical momentum around thalidomide analogues rests on it. I would put Handa ahead of Ciulli in a three-person cut, though I accept Ciulli's VHL ligands were essential to making PROTACs drug-like. I also doubt sequencing is more mature in a way that outweighs conceptual novelty, since the Nobel Committee for Medicine and the Chemistry prize have both honoured sequencing-adjacent work before.

responses.point: Aqvist puts prime editing (Liu, possibly with Anzalone) first as a designed, protein-engineering and RNA-guided chemistry achievement, and ranks degradation only fifth.
responses.response: I respect the engineering elegance of prime editing, but I would hold it back. It is a younger invention than base editing and has far thinner clinical evidence, and a genome-editing prize so soon after 2020 invites a maturity objection. Degradation has more independent confirmation and a longer mechanistic record, and it already has human proof-of-concept. If the committee wants a Liu prize, base editing is the better-attested candidate, and I would list it as an alternative rather than prime editing.

responses.point: Sparr ranks ionizable lipid nanoparticles first, centred on Cullis, Hope and Madden and on lipid self-assembly and bilayer phase behaviour.
responses.response: This is the strongest competing case, and I ranked it second myself. The self-assembly science is real and the societal reach is extraordinary. My reservations are attribution and overlap. The credit is spread across Cullis, Hope, Madden, MacLachlan, Anderson and Langer, and the 2023 Medicine prize already honoured the mRNA side. I would not call it less meritorious, only harder to define in three names. If the committee settles the Vancouver allocation, I would be comfortable moving it to first place.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks proton-coupled electron transfer first, as a unifying principle in respiration, photosynthesis and electrocatalysis, with degradation second.
responses.response: I take his point that PCET has deep conceptual reach across biology and fuel chemistry, and that it is less exposed to a clinical-maturity objection than degradation. My hesitation is that its credit is split between experiment and theory (Mayer, Hammes-Schiffer, Nocera, Meyer) and that its recognition would be mostly within physical and inorganic chemistry. I do not read that as a defect. I do think the degradation prize connects more directly to the molecular-design theme that the committee has recently rewarded.

uncertainties: Whether the prize should honour PROTAC design, the cereblon/molecular-glue mechanism, or both
Whether Handa or Ciulli should hold the third place, and how Ito, Gray and Sakamoto are treated
Whether the absence of an approved degrader makes the prize premature
Whether base editing or ionizable lipids would be preferable if the committee prefers a more clinically mature achievement
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I have no documented personal or institutional tie to the PROTAC, cereblon, lipid nanoparticle or base-editing groups. My peptide, nanoparticle and biosensor research is not directly connected to any of these candidates.
